title: How AI Has Tech Companies Pivoting
author: Eleanor Lightbody · Zach Abramowitz

dom.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source addresses legal-AI reliability through abstention, specialist data and model safeguards, but does not assess whether automation undermines associate apprenticeship or how training should be reconstructed. Its safeguards are relevant to safer AI use, yet they do not establish a position on the cluster’s principal training proposition.
qs: So you've really just hit like home and what makes us different is that we kind of, we've understood that from day one and if you're working with lawyers, it's okay to tell the lawyers and it's okay for the AI to tell the lawyers that it doesn't know the answer.
I think that being a domain expert and building a specialist AI system for lawyers, we believe is so important.

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: The source only forecasts the presence of certain organisations or events and provides no substantive view on user-led legal AI adoption, autonomy, verification, market transformation, or skills and governance. There is insufficient evidence to determine its position relative to the cluster proposition.

st.t: Vendor strategy: Faster building cannot eliminate integration
st.an: The source supports a narrower cluster point about corporate-customer growth and a possible move toward contract analysis, but it does not address whether faster AI-enabled development changes build-versus-buy economics or leaves integration, migration and adoption as slower constraints. The strategic-shift framing also comes chiefly from the interviewer and receives only a general affirmation.
qs: The last year alone, those teams, well, those in-house teams that are buying a corporate product, that has doubled in the amount of customers that we welcomed.

And now, from what I can tell from listening to other interviews you've done, the company is moving much more into what I would call the contract lifecycle management space, but really trying to fill a role on the data extraction, sort of understanding what's in your contracts.

st.t: Vendor value: Concentration forecasts face diverse competition
st.an: The source reports Luminance’s $75 million fundraising and Lightbody’s personal experience of AI disrupting a legacy-provider market, but it does not assess durable value capture, competitive concentration, legal-AI performance, retention, revenue quality or investment returns. It therefore neither substantiates nor rejects the cluster’s proposition.
qs: We talked about all things AI and legal, but what we did not talk about was the news that Luminance released shortly after Eleanor sat down with me, which is that they've raised $75 million in new capital.
I saw firsthand how transformative AI could be in an industry that at the time was pretty run by legacy providers.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s strategy-led approach by proposing a concrete organisational structure: ring-fence exploratory capacity while maintaining a team focused on current customer needs, then blend the two. Its forecast of diminishing human review is speculative and creates tension with the cluster’s emphasis on verification, but does not displace its broader case for selective, practical adaptation.
qs: But actually it's important to have a few people ring-fenced off, because actually contracting might change.
And so you've got to blend both of them together.

st.t: Workflow trust: Verification remains costly and contested
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that legal AI need not be error-free if it handles uncertainty transparently, and materially extends the trust-building mechanisms with specialist models and diverse, lawyer-tagged legal data. Its claimed hallucination reduction is a design rationale rather than measured evidence, and it does not address verification costs or broader organisational governance.
qs: We believe that there are certain things when you're working with lawyers, that you need to have accuracy and you need to like, it's okay if the AI sometimes tells the end user that it doesn't know the answer.

So the fact that the early years, for five years we were working with law firms, we were getting contracts that have been tagged by some of the best lawyers in the world, and we have a rich data set that has a huge amount of variety.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source supports the proposition that dependable legal AI requires more than general model capability: it emphasises domain expertise, lawyer-tagged data and safeguards such as abstaining when uncertain. It does not establish effectiveness through measured results or address the full agentic-workflow and human-checkpoint framework.
qs: It's important to say that once we all are super focused on the models, it's not just about the models, it's about the data as well.
I think that being a domain expert and building a specialist AI system for lawyers, we believe is so important.

st.t: Contract intelligence: Business coordination exceeds document storage
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central shift beyond document storage and one-off review, presenting contracts as business data that legal teams can make accessible and use for value creation. Its end-to-end product and sales self-service example also support the cluster’s business-facing contract-intelligence proposition, although the claims are product-reported rather than outcome-measured.
qs: The conversation has now evolved around or moved and evolved around contracts have so much valuable data in them and actually the legal team are at the center of that.
There's a self-serve that allows, for example, sales teams to create their own contracts.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: The source supports treating in-house legal departments as independent AI customers by reporting unanticipated corporate use of a law-firm-oriented M&A tool for broader contract analysis. It provides anecdotal evidence of latent in-house demand and low-configuration information extraction, but does not establish selective insourcing, reduced outside-counsel spending or measured performance.
qs: I suppose I came in however many years ago and I noticed with a few of us, myself and the founders, that we had quite a few in-house legal teams who were using our M&A tool.
They said, well, you're the only technology that you can put in 100 contracts, you can put in a million contracts, and I can get key information.

st.t: Legal data: Connected records enable operational transformation
st.an: The source supports the proposition that usable contract data can create business value and shift some legal work toward direct business-user access and self-service. It provides product examples and reasoning rather than measured outcomes, and does not materially address selective data preparation, access controls, security or verification.
qs: The conversation has now evolved around or moved and evolved around contracts have so much valuable data in them and actually the legal team are at the center of that.
There's a self-serve that allows, for example, sales teams to create their own contracts.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: The source endorses the cluster’s core proposition that specialist legal AI derives defensible value from domain-specific systems and close engagement with lawyers. It points to lawyer-labelled contract data and law firms’ demanding product testing as differentiators, while offering only company claims and anecdotes rather than comparative performance evidence. It does not materially address the cluster’s broader copilot, verification or accountability proposition.
qs: I think that being a domain expert and building a specialist AI system for lawyers, we believe is so important.
But second to that is they knew that by working with law firms, you could really test the technology, you could really push it because law firms would hold you to the highest standard.

kp.k: Contract review automation originated in repetitive M&A work
kp.d: Lightbody says Luminance's founders responded to lawyers reporting repetitive contract review and data volumes that sometimes forced sampling. Its original combination of supervised and unsupervised machine learning sought to accelerate understanding and identify material lawyers might not know to search for. Abramowitz illustrates the previous workflow through his own frequent use of Ctrl F, rather than presenting systematic evidence.
qs: a lot of them, especially M&A lawyers were sitting and reviewing very similar contracts and sometimes having to even sample those documents because they just didn't have enough hours in day to get through all of that data.
it was a blend of supervised and unsupervised machine learning, which allowed the end user, lawyers, to understand their contracts faster.
I used to press Ctrl F as a M&A attorney, you know, 250 plus times a day.

kp.k: In-house demand prompted expansion beyond M&A review
kp.d: Lightbody attributes the corporate-product pivot to in-house teams already using Luminance's M&A tool despite its mismatch with their workflows. In her account, those customers valued extracting information at scale without manually maintaining metadata or writing rules, including answering questions about force majeure and uncapped liability. She says the corporate product was built three years before the interview.
qs: we had quite a few in-house legal teams who were using our M&A tool.

They said, well, you're the only technology that you can put in 100 contracts, you can put in a million contracts, and I can get key information. I don't have to update it manually. I don't have to add all this metadata. I don't have to write hard and fast rules for it.
We built that three years ago

kp.k: Contract data positions legal teams as business intelligence providers
kp.d: Lightbody describes a shift from occasional risk inquiries toward ongoing exploitation of contractual data, including termination-for-convenience and auto-renewal provisions. She argues that legal teams can use this information to add business value and respond to changing regulation and compliance needs. Separately, Abramowitz argues that access to contract information should not depend on an army of lawyers and paralegals.
qs: But now it's like, where are the terminations for convenience? Is there auto renewal?
contracts have so much valuable data in them and actually the legal team are at the center of that. How can they use that data? How can they mine it to add value to businesses?
It shouldn't be that the thing that separates you from that information is an army of attorneys and paralegals.

kp.k: Self-service and embedded AI redistribute contracting tasks
kp.d: Lightbody describes a corporate product spanning contract creation, negotiation and repository workflows. Sales teams can create contracts themselves, while lawyers can use a Microsoft Word integration either to rewrite a contract toward company standards or receive clause-level acceptability signals and proposed language. These are vendor descriptions of functionality, including both automation and lawyer-in-the-loop review.
qs: There's a self-serve that allows, for example, sales teams to create their own contracts.
they can use Luminance within Microsoft Word, click a button and the AI will rewrite the whole contract to be more aligned with their standards.
Yellow and red are yellow, not sure you need to review and red is something you would never agree to. Then the AI gives you language that you should use instead.
Then you save it onto the repository and there you've got all the automated workflows, you've got total insights into your contractual landscape.

kp.k: Full automation remains limited to certain contracts
kp.d: Despite an end-to-end automation ambition, Lightbody explicitly says only a small subset of contracts, such as NDAs, can be fully automated. For other contracts she frames AI as augmenting workflows and accelerating negotiation or information retrieval, rather than universally replacing legal involvement.
qs: But then also we understand that not all contracts can be automated end to end. Actually only a small section of those can be like an NDA.
But so let's augment the workflows as well to any other contracts that are coming in.

How can we accelerate and speed up whether it's negotiation times up to 90 percent on given negotiations or is it finding things within contracts, or is it finding things you didn't know existed within your contracts?

kp.k: Customer examples claim substantial contracting time savings
kp.d: Lightbody reports that the customer transcribed as Hotachi reduced NDA generation and sign-off from a day or so to five minutes through sales self-service; AMD saved up to 90 percent on NDA reviews using automated rewriting; and Yokogawa reduced business-question response times from five to seven working days to 15 minutes maximum. These are vendor-reported customer examples; the transcript provides no study design or sample sizes.
qs: you've got Hotachi, one of our customers who used to take them a day or so to generate a contract, create it and get it signed off. Now, the sales teams do that all themselves, and they've reduced it down to five minutes per NDA.
They saved up to 90 percent on those reviews, so they can focus on other things.
Or you've got the repository, which is something like Yokogawa. It used to take them five to seven working days to answer business questions.
Now, it takes them 15 minutes at a maximum to answer business questions

kp.k: Adoption reflects changing appetites as well as technical capability
kp.d: Abramowitz frames generative AI as making corporate technology adoption more mainstream, and Lightbody agrees. She characterizes legal technology as moving from optional to necessary for productivity, efficiency and discovering otherwise hidden information. As company-level indicators, the host reports $75 million in new capital announced after the interview, while Lightbody reports 5X growth over two years and a doubling in corporate-product customers welcomed over the last year; the 5X metric is not defined.
qs: they've raised $75 million in new capital.
our growth has grown 5X in the last two years.
The last year alone, those teams, well, those in-house teams that are buying a corporate product, that has doubled in the amount of customers that we welcomed.
this is definitely a must-have, we need to be using technology to help us increase productivity, to help increase efficiencies

kp.k: Law-firm relationships supply data and demanding validation
kp.d: Lightbody says Luminance initially sold only to law firms to obtain lawyer-tagged contracts and test the technology against demanding users, with trust and validation intended to support later in-house expansion. She presents a varied dataset developed through five years of law-firm work as a basis for specialist AI differentiation.
qs: by working with law firms, you could really test the technology, you could really push it because law firms would hold you to the highest standard.
If you can build trust with them, then when you step into the in-house legal team, legal market, then hopefully, you validated your approach, you validated and you've got that trust.
for five years we were working with law firms, we were getting contracts that have been tagged by some of the best lawyers in the world, and we have a rich data set that has a huge amount of variety.

kp.k: Specialist model ensembles aim to constrain unreliable answers
kp.d: Lightbody describes combining foundational, open-source and internally built models in a 'panel of judges' that exploits different strengths and seeks consensus. She emphasizes allowing the system to admit uncertainty rather than invent answers, and claims specialist data and safeguards reduce hallucinations. This is an architectural rationale and vendor claim, not a reported benchmark or quantified error-rate finding; model self-checking is distinct from human verification.
qs: you want to build a panel of experts underneath the hood that use a combination of foundational models, combination of some open source models, some models that we've built ourselves.
it's okay for the AI to tell the lawyers that it doesn't know the answer.
Actually, that's even more important than making up an answer and feeling that you're pleasing it, but it's not necessarily an answer that can be trusted.
You feed those into the models, then you can provide the safeguards to limit and totally reduce hallucinations.

kp.k: Separate development teams address present workflows and future uncertainty
kp.d: Responding to Abramowitz's question about rapidly changing software habits, Lightbody recommends balancing current customer feedback with protected future-oriented development. She says Luminance has a Cambridge 'blue sky' team largely disconnected from customer feedback, alongside a team focused on current expectations. Her landline/mobile-phone analogy supports the argument that existing users may not anticipate radically different possibilities.
qs: you want to make sure that you have a good balance of building for the customer and the customer feedback that you're getting today, but also having a team that's only focused on tomorrow.
They probably have no idea what our customer's feedback is, but that's okay, because they're building for a different world.
it's important to have a few people ring-fenced off, because actually contracting might change.

kp.k: Future NDA negotiations may dispense with human review
kp.d: Lightbody speculates that within five years contracting could involve AI on both sides, with humans reviewing only summaries or eventually not reviewing even those if trust becomes sufficient. She qualifies this vision by referring to NDAs or similar contracts and expresses personal willingness to delegate NDA negotiation. This is a conditional future shift from augmentation toward direct reliance, not evidence of widespread current autonomous practice.
qs: In the next five years, we might not have a contract the way that we know it.
You might have AI either side and actually you are only reviewing the summary, or even that you might decide in time not to even review the summary, because you have so much trust in the AI.
Again, this is for NDAs and NDAs or something like that, where quite frankly, I'd be very happy if AI negotiated the NDAs, I have to look at on a daily basis, and I trust the AI will do that.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Eleanor Lightbody claims AI makes large contract collections intelligible faster and enables legal departments to use contractual data for business value and compliance.
pts.d: Lightbody describes Luminance's development from an M&A review tool into a corporate contracting product. She claims its original supervised and unsupervised machine-learning system identified concepts and clauses, including material users did not know existed. Its corporate product combines contract analysis, a repository and automated workflows to surface business-relevant information such as termination and renewal provisions, while helping companies respond to regulatory change.

pts.k: Lightbody claims AI can automate selected contracting tasks and augment the rest, including business-user self-service and contract rewriting.
pts.d: She describes sales teams creating contracts themselves, lawyers using a Microsoft Word integration to rewrite contracts toward company standards, and an alternative review mode that flags acceptable, uncertain and unacceptable clauses and proposes replacement language. She expressly limits complete end-to-end automation to a small subset of contracts, such as NDAs; other contracts remain workflows that AI accelerates rather than fully replaces.

pts.k: Lightbody claims specialist legal AI, combining multiple models and lawyer-tagged data, can reduce hallucinations and avoid unsupported answers.
pts.d: She attributes Luminance's differentiation to a 'panel of experts' combining foundational models, open-source models and internally built models, with consensus and the ability to decline an answer. She also identifies contracts tagged by lawyers during the company's early law-firm work as a source of safeguards. This is a claim about system design and reliability, not a reported benchmark result or evidence that human verification is unnecessary.

pts.k: Lightbody claims legal technology has shifted from optional to essential, with rapid demonstrable value supporting corporate adoption.
pts.d: She presents productivity, efficiency, potential time and cost reductions, and previously hidden contract insights as adoption drivers and sources of competitive advantage. She says most customers sign up after a two-week trial because they can establish a business case. These are her market interpretation and vendor adoption claims, rather than quantified findings about the legal market as a whole.

pts.k: Lightbody predicts that AI-to-AI negotiation could change the form of contracting, with people reviewing only summaries or eventually reviewing nothing for routine agreements.
pts.d: She presents this as a possible future, not an established capability across contracting. Her example is NDAs and similar agreements, contingent on users developing sufficient trust in AI. This envisages movement from lawyer augmentation toward direct reliance on AI-negotiated outcomes. She links that possibility to maintaining a separate future-focused development team alongside teams responding to current customer needs.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Lightbody supports productivity claims with named customer examples and reported time savings.
pts.d: She reports that the customer rendered as 'Hotachi' in the transcript reduced NDA generation and sign-off from roughly a day to five minutes through sales-team self-service. She attributes savings of up to 90 percent on NDA reviews to AMD's use of AI rewriting within Word, and says Yokogawa reduced business-question response times from five to seven working days to a maximum of 15 minutes. These are vendor-reported customer cases; the interview supplies no measurement methodology, sample sizes or independent validation.

pts.k: The reliability claim rests on Lightbody's account of technical architecture, specialist data and experience with demanding law-firm users.
pts.d: Lightbody says early law-firm customers supplied high-quality tagged contracts and subjected the product to demanding use, supporting its later move into corporate legal departments. She offers this development history as the basis for trust and differentiation. No measured hallucination rates, model comparisons, accuracy figures or formal test results are provided.

pts.k: Lightbody cites company growth and trial experience as indicators of demand, without supplying market-wide adoption data.
pts.d: She reports fivefold growth over two years, without clearly identifying the growth metric, and a doubling over the preceding year in the number of corporate-product customers welcomed. Her two-week trial conversion account is not accompanied by a numerical conversion rate or customer count. These statements concern Luminance, a software vendor, rather than an alternative legal service provider delivering legal work.

pts.k: The AI-to-AI contracting forecast is supported by strategic reasoning and personal willingness to delegate NDAs, not a reported deployment study.
pts.d: Lightbody describes a Cambridge 'blue sky' team insulated from current customer feedback and uses the transition from landlines to mobile phones to illustrate why customers may not anticipate future interactions. These explain her innovation strategy but do not constitute empirical evidence for the predicted change in contracting.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Lightbody distinguishes current contracting capabilities from a conditional five-year vision of more autonomous contracting.
pts.d: At the interview dated 2025, she describes the corporate product as built three years earlier and its customer benefits as already occurring. Reported review savings are 'up to' 90 percent for particular uses, not universal guarantees. Full end-to-end automation currently applies only to a small subset of contracts; broader workflows are augmented. Her prediction of changed contracting is framed as a possibility within five years, approximately 2030, while dispensing with even summary review is described less precisely as occurring 'in time' and depending on trust.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims principally concern corporate legal departments, business teams and enterprises, with law firms as early users and legal-tech vendors adapting their products.
pts.d: M&A lawyers gain faster document review and discovery of contractual provisions. In-house lawyers gain automated drafting and review assistance, faster responses to business questions and opportunities to use contract data strategically. Sales teams can generate routine contracts without routing every step through legal. Businesses obtain faster contracting, better visibility into obligations and risks, and possible efficiency advantages. Legal-tech vendors must develop both current workflow tools and future AI-native interactions. Lightbody does not make a concrete prediction of lawyer job losses, staffing changes or improved public access to justice.
